learning_outcomes.text: Provide knowledge on general scientific contents and methodological-operational aspects of fluid mechanics.
Provide knowledge of the fundamental equations governing the motion of a fluid.
Acquire the ability to properly size fluid systems governed by a simple one-dimensional balance.
Description of the matter as a continuum.
Fluid statics.
Balance equations on a finite volume.
Balance equations on an infinitesimal volume.
Bernoulli's Law.
Currents with negligible acceleration.
Potential flow.
Boundary layer flow.
Turbulent flow in ducts.
To properly size those fluid systems whose characteristics derive from a simple one-dimensional balance.
To determine forces and torques acting on systems in contact with a fluid at rest or in motion.
To derive the basic dimensionless parameters that determine the behaviour and the performances of a fluid system.
To obtain an overview of the different behaviours that a fluid can manifest, describing in a simplified manner (both qualitatively and quantitatively) their main features.
To acquire and use a scientific terminology appropriate to describe and model a fluid system.
Evaluate the importance of different physical mechanisms in typical fluid mechanics applications, being able to qualitatively predict the main phenomenological aspects.
Clearly and accurately communicate complex concepts related to fluid mechanics using appropriate technical language.
Describe physical phenomena, equations, and results of fluid dynamic analysis in an understandable manner.
Active listening, the ability to express opinions clearly, and effective teamwork.
Learn the basic principles of fluid mechanics, including concepts such as fluid statics and dynamics, fluid properties, and the fundamental laws governing fluid behavior.
Model and analyze fluid flows in various regimes, such as laminar and turbulent flows, steady-state and transient regimes.
Solve a variety of engineering problems, ranging from determining the forces acting on bodies immersed in fluids to the design principles of complex flow systems.

Solve simple problems in fluid dynamics by identifying the data needed, choosing an appropriate mathematical model, outlining a clear solution procedure, and performing formal and numerical calculations with confidence.

syllabus_topics: The description of the matter as a continuum: Local mechanical invariants, Balance equations, Properties of fluids, General form of the momentum flux, Mass and surface forces, Stress tensor.
Fluid statics: Equation of hydrostatics, Manometers, Forces acting on surfaces.
Balance equations on a finite volume: Reynolds transport theorem, Conservation of mass, Momentum and angular momentum with applications, Dimensional analysis.

Balance equations on an infinitesimal volume: Material derivative, Newton's law of viscosity, Euler and Navier-Stokes equations, Streamlines and their representation, Maximum of motion flows, Exact solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations.
Bernoulli's law: Static, Dynamic and total pressure, Hydraulic head, Head losses, Venturi tube.
Currents with negligible acceleration: Reynolds' theory of lubrication, Stokes flow around a sphere and a cylinder.
Potential flow: Flow fields obtainable as a superposition of simple solution (source/sink, vortex, doublet), Generation of lift, Lift and drag coefficients.
The boundary layer: Concept of similarity, Boundary layer on a flat plate and drag evaluation, Qualitative description of the phenomena associated with separation.
Turbulent flow in ducts: Properties of turbulence, Velocity profile, Prandtl's law of friction, Moody diagram, Losses in straight ducts, Pipe fittings, Flow measurements.
Overview of the course and final exercises.
teaching_methods: Practice classes (problem solving, discussions, movie projections)

assessment_methods.method: Written exam (open-ended and/or multiple-choice questions on theoretical aspects)
Written exam (practical exercises solving applied problems)

assessment_rules: The final grade, expressed on a thirty-point scale, will consider the level of knowledge and understanding of theoretical aspects, the ability to apply acquired knowledge to problem-solving, and the correctness, completeness, and clarity of written work, including presentation quality and use of scientific terminology. The minimum passing grade is 18/30. Higher grades are awarded for thorough mastery, independent application of knowledge, methodological rigor, clear presentation, and ability to solve complex problems.
